william-henry-bartlett.name: William Henry Bartlett
william-henry-bartlett.summary: British artist (1809–1854) known for drawings rendered into steel engravings.

barada.name: Barada River
barada.summary: The main river of Damascus, the capital city of Syria.

date-honey.name: Dibs (date syrup)
date-honey.summary: A thick, dark, very sweet syrup pressed from dates, also called date honey or date molasses, widely used in Middle Eastern, North African and South Asian cooking.

robert-koldewey.name: Robert Koldewey
robert-koldewey.summary: German archaeologist (1855-1925) who led the excavation of ancient Babylon from 1899, uncovering the Ishtar Gate and developing techniques for excavating mudbrick architecture like the Hanging Gardens.

nebuchadnezzar-ii.name: Nebuchadnezzar II
nebuchadnezzar-ii.summary: Second king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, ruling 605 to 562 BC; renowned for military victories including Carchemish and for major construction projects in Babylon.

ishtar-gate.name: Ishtar Gate
ishtar-gate.summary: The eighth gate of Babylon's inner city wall, built around 569 BC under King Nebuchadnezzar II, decorated with glazed-brick animals and deities; excavated by Robert Koldewey from 1904 to 1914.

claudius-rich.name: Claudius Rich
claudius-rich.summary: A British Assyriologist, business agent, traveller and antiquarian scholar who lived from 1787 to 1821.

staatliche-museen-zu-berlin.name: Royal Museums of Berlin
staatliche-museen-zu-berlin.summary: Founded in 1823 by King Friedrich Wilhelm III of Prussia as the Royal Museums, it later grew into the Berlin State Museums, now the largest museum complex in Europe.

etemenanki.name: Etemenanki
etemenanki.summary: A Babylonian ziggurat dedicated to the god Marduk, now in ruins near Baghdad, sometimes linked to the biblical Tower of Babel.

fao-landing.name: Fao Landing
fao-landing.summary: A British military operation against Ottoman forces at Fao in November 1914, the first action of the Mesopotamian Campaign in World War I, undertaken to protect British oil supplies.

anglo-persian-oil-company.name: Anglo-Persian Oil Company
anglo-persian-oil-company.summary: A British company founded in 1909 after a major oil discovery in Persia; the British government took a controlling 51% stake in 1914, and it later became British Petroleum.

khuzestan-province.name: Khuzestan province
khuzestan-province.summary: A province in southwestern Iran bordering Iraq and the Persian Gulf, corresponding to ancient Elam whose capital was Susa; it holds Iran's largest oil field.

shatt-al-arab.name: Shatt al-Arab
shatt-al-arab.summary: A roughly 200-kilometre river formed where the Euphrates and Tigris meet in southern Iraq, flowing into the Persian Gulf and forming part of the Iran–Iraq border.

sinai-and-palestine-campaign.name: Sinai and Palestine campaign
sinai-and-palestine-campaign.summary: A World War I campaign (1915–1918) in which the British Empire and allies fought the Ottoman Empire, ending with the Ottomans' loss of Syria.

caucasus-campaign.name: Caucasus campaign
caucasus-campaign.summary: A World War I campaign fought mainly between the Russian and Ottoman empires across the South Caucasus and Armenian Highlands, part of the Middle Eastern theatre.

abdulaziz-bin-muhammad-al-saud.name: Abdulaziz bin Muhammad Al Saud
abdulaziz-bin-muhammad-al-saud.summary: Second ruler of the Emirate of Diriyah, reigning 1765–1803, son of its founder Muhammad bin Saud and son-in-law of Muhammad bin Abdul Wahhab; nicknamed the 'savior of his time.'

husayn-ibn-ali.name: Husayn ibn Ali
husayn-ibn-ali.summary: Grandson of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and the third Shia Imam (626-680), who refused to pledge allegiance to the caliph Yazid after his father's death.

siirt.name: Siirt
siirt.summary: A city in southeastern Turkey with a population of about 160,000 in 2021, predominantly inhabited by Kurds.

german-ottoman-alliance.name: German–Ottoman alliance
german-ottoman-alliance.summary: A 1914 alliance between the German and Ottoman Empires, formed to strengthen the Ottoman military and give Germany access to nearby British colonies.

paul-bronsart-von-schellendorff.name: Paul Bronsart von Schellendorff
paul-bronsart-von-schellendorff.summary: A Prussian general and writer (1832-1891) who served as Minister of War from 1883 to 1889.

lord-byron.name: Lord Byron
lord-byron.summary: A British Romantic poet (1788–1824) known for works like Don Juan and Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, who died in 1824 from a fever while leading a campaign in the Greek War of Independence.

psalm-137.name: Psalm 137
psalm-137.summary: A psalm from the Book of Psalms beginning 'By the rivers of Babylon,' lamenting exile and longing for Jerusalem during the Babylonian captivity; still used in Jewish and Christian liturgy today.

hebrew-melodies.name: Hebrew Melodies
hebrew-melodies.summary: A collection of 30 poems by Lord Byron, largely written to accompany music composed by Isaac Nathan.

babylonian-captivity.name: Babylonian captivity
babylonian-captivity.summary: The exile of Judeans from the Kingdom of Judah to Babylonia by the Neo-Babylonian Empire after sieges of Jerusalem in 597 and 587 BCE, ending when Persia allowed their return in 539 BCE.

giuseppe-verdi.name: Giuseppe Verdi
giuseppe-verdi.summary: An Italian composer (1813–1901) who dominated 19th-century opera, becoming a symbol of Italy's unification movement through works such as Nabucco.

nabucco.name: Nabucco
nabucco.summary: An 1841 Italian opera by Giuseppe Verdi about the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II and the exile of the Jews, credited with establishing Verdi's reputation.

va-pensiero.name: Va, pensiero
va-pensiero.summary: A chorus from Giuseppe Verdi's 1842 opera Nabucco, also known as the "Chorus of the Hebrew Slaves," inspired by Psalm 137 and depicting Babylonian captivity.

girsu.name: Girsu
girsu.summary: An ancient Sumerian city about 25 km northwest of Lagash, in what is now Iraq, that served as Lagash's religious center with major temples to the god Ningirsu.

eshnunna.name: Eshnunna
eshnunna.summary: An ancient Sumerian, later Akkadian, city-state in the Diyala Valley of central Mesopotamia, northwest of Sumer proper.

khafajah.name: Khafajah
khafajah.summary: An archaeological site in Iraq, ancient Tutub, occupied from the Uruk period through the Old Babylonian Empire and controlled successively by the Akkadian Empire and the Third Dynasty of Ur.

ur.name: Ur
ur.summary: A major Sumerian city-state in ancient Mesopotamia dating from about 3800 BC, whose patron deity was the moon god Nanna and whose ziggurat still stands partially restored.

cuneiform.name: Cuneiform
cuneiform.summary: The earliest known writing system, made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay, developed for Sumerian and later adapted for Akkadian and other ancient Near Eastern languages.

adolf-b-ttger.name: Adolf Böttger
adolf-b-ttger.summary: German translator and poet (1815–1870) best known for translating Byron's complete works into German.

isaac-nathan.name: Isaac Nathan
isaac-nathan.summary: Anglo-Jewish Australian composer (1792–1864) called the 'father of Australian music,' known for his Hebrew Melodies and for writing Australia's first operas.

carl-loewe.name: Carl Loewe
carl-loewe.summary: German composer, tenor and conductor (1796–1869) whose many ballads and songs led some to call him the "Schubert of North Germany".

charles-valentin-alkan.name: Charles-Valentin Alkan
charles-valentin-alkan.summary: French composer and virtuoso pianist (1813–1888) who ranked alongside Chopin and Liszt among Paris's leading pianists, though he lived reclusively for much of his later career.

charles-gounod.name: Charles Gounod
charles-gounod.summary: French Romantic-era composer, conductor and organist (1818–1893) best known for his opera Faust and for church music including his Ave Maria.

henry-brougham-farnie.name: Henry Brougham Farnie
henry-brougham-farnie.summary: British librettist and journalist (1836 to 1889) whose English adaptations of French operettas became record-setting hits on the London stage.

ferruccio-busoni.name: Ferruccio Busoni
ferruccio-busoni.summary: An Italian composer, pianist, conductor and teacher (1866-1924) who worked closely with leading musicians of his era and developed an individual, sometimes atonal style after 1907.

hejaz-railway.name: Hejaz railway
hejaz-railway.summary: A narrow-gauge railway built by the Ottoman Empire from 1900, running from Damascus to Medina with a branch to Haifa, meant to link Istanbul with the Islamic holy cities.

abdul-hamid-ii.name: Abdul Hamid II
abdul-hamid-ii.summary: 34th sultan of the Ottoman Empire (1876–1909), the last to hold effective control over the fracturing state, who suspended the constitution in 1878 and ruled with absolute power.

austen-henry-layard.name: Austen Henry Layard
austen-henry-layard.summary: British archaeologist, diplomat and politician (1817–1894) who excavated Nimrud and Nineveh, uncovering Assyrian palace reliefs and the library of Ashurbanipal, most now in the British Museum.

daniel-bliss.name: Daniel Bliss
daniel-bliss.summary: American Christian missionary (1823–1916) who founded the American University of Beirut.

berlin-baghdad-railway.name: Baghdad railway
berlin-baghdad-railway.summary: A railway begun in 1903 to link Berlin to Ottoman Baghdad through modern Turkey, Syria and Iraq, funded mainly by Germany but not fully completed until 1940.

nineveh.name: Nineveh
nineveh.summary: Ancient city on the Tigris near modern Mosul, Iraq, and capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire; briefly the largest city in the world until it was sacked in 612 BC.

neo-assyrian-empire.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
neo-assyrian-empire.summary: An ancient Mesopotamian empire beginning in 911 BCE that grew to dominate the Near East, Egypt and parts of Anatolia, described as history's first world empire.

american-university-of-beirut.name: American University of Beirut
american-university-of-beirut.summary: A private, non-sectarian university in Beirut, Lebanon, chartered in New York and offering degrees through the PhD level; originally founded as the Syrian Protestant College.

aley.name: Aley
aley.summary: A major city in central Lebanon, on Mount Lebanon about 15 km uphill from Beirut, nicknamed the "Bride of the Summer resorts" for its cool climate.

souk-el-gharb.name: Souk-al-Gharb
souk-el-gharb.summary: A town in Lebanon's Aley District, once a prosperous mountain resort before the 1975–1990 civil war, now considered a suburb of Aley.

philipp-holzmann.name: Philipp Holzmann
philipp-holzmann.summary: German construction company based in Frankfurt am Main.

chemins-de-fer-ottomans-d-anatolie.name: Anatolian Railway
chemins-de-fer-ottomans-d-anatolie.summary: An Ottoman railway company founded in 1888, the busiest line in the empire, linking Istanbul to Ankara and Konya; it was financed by Germany's Deutsche Bank.

jarabulus.name: Jarabulus
jarabulus.summary: A Syrian city on the Euphrates' western bank near the Turkish border, part of Aleppo Governorate, with a population of about 11,570 in the 2004 census.

tripoli-lebanon.name: Tripoli, Lebanon
tripoli-lebanon.summary: The largest city in northern Lebanon and a Mediterranean seaport, with a history dating back at least to the 14th century BC and known historically as Tripoli of the Levant.

muhammad-ali-of-egypt.name: Muhammad Ali of Egypt
muhammad-ali-of-egypt.summary: An Ottoman governor of Albanian origin who became de facto ruler of Egypt from 1805 to 1848, widely considered the founder of modern Egypt.

ibrahim-pasha-of-egypt.name: Ibrahim Pasha
ibrahim-pasha-of-egypt.summary: An Egyptian general and the eldest son of Muhammad Ali, who commanded Egyptian and Ottoman armies and briefly ruled Egypt and Sudan as regent before dying only four months later, in 1848.

mahmud-ii.name: Mahmud II
mahmud-ii.summary: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1808 to 1839 who abolished the conservative Janissary Corps and pushed major reforms, though the empire kept losing territory.

ottoman-syria.name: Ottoman Syria
ottoman-syria.summary: Historiographical term for the Ottoman Empire's provinces in the Levant, organized after the conquest from the Mamluks in the early 16th century and later reorganized into several vilayets.

damascus-affair.name: Damascus affair
damascus-affair.summary: A February 1840 case in which Jews in Damascus were tortured into false murder confessions after a monk's disappearance, encouraged by French consul Ratti-Menton, sparking international outrage.

egyptian-ottoman-war-1839-1841.name: Second Egyptian–Ottoman War
egyptian-ottoman-war-1839-1841.summary: An 1839–1841 war fought mainly in Syria, ending when Muhammad Ali gave up his claims there in return for his family's recognition as Egypt's rulers.

moses-montefiore.name: Moses Montefiore
moses-montefiore.summary: British financier, banker and philanthropist (1784–1885) who funded Jewish settlement and development in the Levant, seen as pivotal to early Zionism.

adolphe-cr-mieux.name: Adolphe Crémieux
adolphe-cr-mieux.summary: French lawyer and politician (1796–1880) who served as Minister of Justice and secured French citizenship for Algerian Jews through the Crémieux Decree.

abd-lmecid-i.name: Abdülmecid I
abd-lmecid-i.summary: 31st sultan of the Ottoman Empire (1839–1861) whose Tanzimat Edict launched an era of reform and closer ties with Britain and France, including alliance in the Crimean War.

russo-turkish-war-1877-1878.name: Russo-Turkish War of 1877-78
russo-turkish-war-1877-1878.summary: A war in which Russia and Balkan allies defeated the Ottoman Empire, leading to Romanian, Serbian and Montenegrin independence and Bulgarian autonomy.

ottoman-public-debt-administration.name: Ottoman Public Debt Administration
ottoman-public-debt-administration.summary: European-run body set up in 1881 to collect Ottoman debts owed to foreign creditors, growing into a bureaucracy of thousands that financed railways and other projects.

alexander-hislop.name: Alexander Hislop
alexander-hislop.summary: A Free Church of Scotland minister (1807-1865) and critic of the Catholic Church, best known for his book The Two Babylons, arguing Catholic practices descended from ancient Babylon.

the-two-babylons.name: The Two Babylons
the-two-babylons.summary: An 1853 book by Presbyterian theologian Alexander Hislop (1807–1865) arguing that the Catholic Church is the Babylon of Revelation and that its holidays descend from pagan festivals; modern scholars reject its arguments.

leonard-william-king.name: Leonard William King
leonard-william-king.summary: An English archaeologist and Assyriologist (1869–1919) who collected Near Eastern inscriptions, taught Assyrian and Babylonian archaeology, translated works such as the Code of Hammurabi, and served at the British Museum.

babylonian-religion-and-mythology.name: Babylonian Religion and Mythology
babylonian-religion-and-mythology.summary: A 1899 scholarly book by English Assyriologist L. W. King analyzing the religious system of ancient Babylon and its link to Babylonian mythology and thought.

astarte.name: Astarte
astarte.summary: The Hellenized name of the Near Eastern goddess ʿAṯtart, equivalent to Ishtar, worshipped from the Bronze Age through classical antiquity across the Levant and beyond.

inanna.name: Inanna (Ishtar)
inanna.summary: Ancient Mesopotamian goddess of war, love and sex, originally worshipped in Sumer and later known as Ishtar among the Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians.

morris-jastrow-jr.name: Morris Jastrow Jr.
morris-jastrow-jr.summary: Polish-born American orientalist and librarian (1861–1921) associated with the University of Pennsylvania.

marduk.name: Marduk
marduk.summary: The patron god of Babylon, worshipped as a god of creation, justice and magic, who rose to become leader of the Mesopotamian pantheon by the 2nd millennium BC.

enlil.name: Enlil
enlil.summary: Ancient Mesopotamian god of wind, air, earth and storms, chief deity of the Sumerian pantheon, worshipped at the Ekur temple in Nippur from the 24th century BC.

hyperdiffusionism.name: Hyperdiffusionism
hyperdiffusionism.summary: A pseudoarchaeological theory holding that many ancient civilizations' shared technologies and practices spread from a single lost source culture.

theophilus-pinches.name: Theophilus Pinches
theophilus-pinches.summary: An English Assyriologist (1856–1934) who studied ancient Mesopotamian religion and language.

lucian.name: Lucian
lucian.summary: Hellenized Syrian satirist and rhetorician (c. 125–after 180) known for tongue-in-cheek writings mocking philosophers and superstitions, written in Greek though his native language was probably Syriac.

on-the-syrian-goddess.name: On the Syrian Goddess
on-the-syrian-goddess.summary: Second-century Greek treatise describing religious cults practiced at the temple of Hierapolis Bambyce in Syria, traditionally credited to Lucian of Samosata.

julius-oppert.name: Julius Oppert
julius-oppert.summary: French-German Assyriologist born in Hamburg to Jewish parents, who lived from 1825 to 1905.

code-of-hammurabi.name: Code of Hammurabi
code-of-hammurabi.summary: A Babylonian legal text composed around 1753 BC, the longest and best-preserved legal text from the ancient Near East, inscribed on a stele now in the Louvre.

panbabylonism.name: Panbabylonism
panbabylonism.summary: An early 20th-century school of thought, mainly among German Assyriologists, holding that Middle Eastern cultures and religions derived from Babylonian astronomy and myth.

christogram.name: IHS
christogram.summary: One of several abbreviations of the Greek spelling of the name Jesus, used since medieval times as a Christian monogram, or Christogram.

horus.name: Horus
horus.summary: Ancient Egyptian falcon-headed deity of kingship, healing, protection, the sun and sky, worshipped from prehistoric Egypt into Roman times and linked to the pharaoh as his living manifestation.

belshazzar.name: Belshazzar
belshazzar.summary: Son and crown prince of Nabonidus, the last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, who served as regent in Babylon during his father's decade-long absence.

nimrod.name: Nimrod
nimrod.summary: Biblical figure in Genesis described as a mighty hunter and king in Shinar, later traditions linking him to the Tower of Babel, though no historical record of him has been found.
